Reference: Assunção et al. (2026)

Model Setting

The paper builds a spatial and dynamic model of efficient land allocation in the Brazilian Amazon biome. Each piece of land can be used for cattle ranching (about 85% of deforested, non-abandoned land is pasture, so agriculture is identified with cattle) or kept as forest. Deforestation releases the carbon stored in primary forest, while abandoned pasture regrows as secondary forest and slowly absorbs carbon. A fictitious social planner, who internalizes the emissions externality, trades off cattle revenue against the value of carbon at an exogenous emissions price. The paper does not model decentralized landowners: since monitoring and enforcement cut deforestation by more than 80% between 2004 and 2012, current deforestation is read as reflecting government valuations, and edge effects and fires make conservation a decision at a scale far above private holdings.

Three ingredients distinguish the analysis from static or discrete-choice models of deforestation (e.g. Souza-Rodrigues (2019), Araujo, Costa and Sant'Anna (2025)): (1) explicit carbon accumulation dynamics in regrowing forests, so that reforestation, not only avoided deforestation, is a choice and transition paths over 15 to 30 years can be computed; (2) large cross-sectional heterogeneity in cattle productivity and carbon density, measured from census and satellite data on 1,043 sites (about 67.5 km by 67.5 km) or 78 coarse sites (about 270 km by 270 km); (3) uncertainty on two fronts: stochastic cattle prices following a Markov chain, and uncertain site productivities, handled with ambiguity aversion toward a baseline Bayesian posterior. The paper first infers a “business-as-usual” shadow price of emissions that rationalizes 1995–2008 deforestation, and then studies how international transfers of bbb dollars per net ton of CO2_22​e captured change land use, carbon and Brazil's welfare.

Land Use and Carbon Dynamics

To handle the asymmetry between clearing and regrowth, the planner chooses two nonnegative site-specific controls: UtiU_t^iUti​ (deforestation) and VtiV_t^iVti​ (reforestation, i.e. abandoning pasture to natural regeneration):

Z˙ti=Uti−Vti,Uti≥0,Vti≥0(9.5.5.2)\dot{Z}_t^i=U_t^i-V_t^i,\qquad U_t^i\ge 0,\quad V_t^i\ge 0 \tag{9.5.5.2}Z˙ti​=Uti​−Vti​,Uti​≥0,Vti​≥0(9.5.5.2)

Carbon captured in site iii evolves as:

X˙ti=−γiUti−α[Xti−γi(zˉi−Zti)](9.5.5.3)\dot{X}_t^i=-\gamma^iU_t^i-\alpha\left[X_t^i-\gamma^i\left(\bar{z}^i-Z_t^i\right)\right] \tag{9.5.5.3}X˙ti​=−γiUti​−α[Xti​−γi(zˉi−Zti​)](9.5.5.3)

The first term is the immediate loss of carbon when primary forest is cleared: γi>0\gamma^i>0γi>0 is the CO2_22​e density of primary forest in site iii (all deforestation is assumed to hit primary forest). The second term is mean reversion of the carbon stock toward its maximum γi(zˉi−Zti)\gamma^i(\bar{z}^i-Z_t^i)γi(zˉi−Zti​), the carbon a fully mature forest would hold on the non-agricultural area. Holding the forest area fixed and setting Ui=0U^i=0Ui=0, the gap closes exponentially, so regrowing forest attains a fraction 1−e−αt1-e^{-\alpha t}1−e−αt of its maximum after ttt years:

Xti−γi(zˉi−Zi)=e−αt[X0i−γi(zˉi−Zi)](9.5.5.4)X_t^i-\gamma^i\left(\bar{z}^i-Z^i\right)=e^{-\alpha t}\left[X_0^i-\gamma^i\left(\bar{z}^i-Z^i\right)\right] \tag{9.5.5.4}Xti​−γi(zˉi−Zi)=e−αt[X0i​−γi(zˉi−Zi)](9.5.5.4)

Following Heinrich et al. (2021), α\alphaα is set so that 99% of the maximum is reached in 100 years (the appendix reports α=0.045\alpha=0.045α=0.045). Initial conditions assume all initial forest is primary, X0i=γi(zˉi−Z0i)X_0^i=\gamma^i(\bar{z}^i-Z_0^i)X0i​=γi(zˉi−Z0i​). The controls satisfy the complementary slackness condition UtiVti=0U_t^iV_t^i=0Uti​Vti​=0: if both were positive, lowering both by Δ\DeltaΔ would raise carbon by γiΔ\gamma^i\DeltaγiΔ today and the extra future emissions from faster depreciation would be worth less because of discounting, so a site is never cleared and regrown simultaneously.

The value of cattle output at site iii is PtaAtiP_t^aA_t^iPta​Ati​, with output proportional to pasture:

Ati=θiZti(9.5.5.5)A_t^i=\theta^iZ_t^i \tag{9.5.5.5}Ati​=θiZti​(9.5.5.5)

where θi\theta^iθi is a site-specific productivity that also absorbs the ratio of local to national prices. Write φi:=(γi,θi)\varphi^i:=(\gamma^i,\theta^i)φi:=(γi,θi) and φ\varphiφ for the full vector. Net emissions of the biome combine emissions from cattle, at rate κ\kappaκ per hectare of pasture (mainly enteric fermentation and soil management), and the change in forest carbon:

Net emissionst=κ∑i=1IZti−∑i=1IX˙ti(9.5.5.6)\text{Net emissions}_t=\kappa\sum_{i=1}^{I}Z_t^i-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\dot{X}_t^i \tag{9.5.5.6}Net emissionst​=κi=1∑I​Zti​−i=1∑I​X˙ti​(9.5.5.6)

Changing land use has quadratic land-use-change costs that depend on the aggregate change across the biome, with separate parameters for clearing and for regrowth:

LCt=ζ12(∑i=1IUti)2+ζ22(∑i=1IVti)2(9.5.5.7)LC_t=\frac{\zeta_1}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{I}U_t^i\right)^2+\frac{\zeta_2}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{I}V_t^i\right)^2 \tag{9.5.5.7}LCt​=2ζ1​​(i=1∑I​Uti​)2+2ζ2​​(i=1∑I​Vti​)2(9.5.5.7)

This is the only explicit interaction across sites: resources for clearing or removing farms are mobile across the Amazon with a less than perfectly elastic supply. Because costs depend on totals rather than site-level changes, the planner prefers to clear or restore one site fully before moving to another; with sites above 4,400 km2^22, optimal paths do not create forest fragments.

Planner's Problem

The planner takes as given an emissions price PeP^ePe, the initial cattle price and the Markov chain. Conditional on productivities φ\varphiφ, the value of a decision process ddd (the whole sequence of controls contingent on price realizations) is:

f(d,φ)=E(∫0∞e−δt[Pta∑i=1IAti−Pe∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)−LCt]dt | φ)(9.5.5.8)f(d,\varphi)=\mathbb{E}\left(\int_0^\infty e^{-\delta t}\left[P_t^a\sum_{i=1}^{I}A_t^i-P^e\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)-LC_t\right]dt\,\middle|\,\varphi\right) \tag{9.5.5.8}f(d,φ)=E(∫0∞​e−δt[Pta​i=1∑I​Ati​−Pei=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)−LCt​]dt​φ)(9.5.5.8)

subject to the dynamics and 0≤Zi≤zˉi0\le Z^i\le\bar{z}^i0≤Zi≤zˉi, with subjective discount rate δ\deltaδ. Agricultural output is valued at sales revenue, i.e. inputs are assumed to have no alternative use; this biases results toward agriculture. The emissions price is decomposed as

Pe=Pee+b(9.5.5.9)P^e=P^{ee}+b \tag{9.5.5.9}Pe=Pee+b(9.5.5.9)

where PeeP^{ee}Pee is Brazil's own business-as-usual shadow price of emissions and bbb is an international transfer payment per ton of net CO2_22​e captured: if net capture is EEE tons, Brazil receives bEbEbE. Payments are made only for net capture; plain conservation is not paid, but net-capture payments implicitly tax deforestation. The model does not track atmospheric carbon stocks.

Productivity Uncertainty and Ambiguity Aversion

Site productivities are not observed directly; they are predicted from regressions and are uncertain. Let π\piπ be a baseline distribution for φ\varphiφ obtained from a tractable Bayesian procedure (an ex ante posterior that serves as the planner's “prior”). The planner does not fully trust π\piπ and performs a penalized sensitivity analysis: it considers alternative densities ggg relative to π\piπ and penalizes them by relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) scaled by ξ\xiξ. The robust planner's problem (Problem 3.1) is a max-min:

max⁡d∈D min⁡g≥0, ∫g dπ=1 ∫f(d,φ) g(φ) dπ(φ)+ξ∫log⁡g(φ) g(φ) dπ(φ)(9.5.5.10)\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\ \min_{g\ge 0,\ \int g\,d\pi=1}\ \int f(d,\varphi)\,g(\varphi)\,d\pi(\varphi)+\xi\int \log g(\varphi)\,g(\varphi)\,d\pi(\varphi) \tag{9.5.5.10}d∈Dmax​ g≥0, ∫gdπ=1min​ ∫f(d,φ)g(φ)dπ(φ)+ξ∫logg(φ)g(φ)dπ(φ)(9.5.5.10)

A larger ξ\xiξ means a larger penalty and less ambiguity aversion; ξ=∞\xi=\inftyξ=∞ is ambiguity neutrality, i.e. full confidence in the baseline posterior. The problem is solved from the vantage point of date zero (a “static” max-min game), so there is no learning about productivities over time.

Productivities are built from two regressions. Let Mi\mathcal{M}^iMi be the set of municipalities intersecting site iii, wmiw_m^iwmi​ the area weight of municipality mmm in site iii, and P2017AP^A_{2017}P2017A​ the 2017 cattle price:

[γiθi]=[exp⁡(βγ⋅Rγi+νγi)1P2017A∑m∈Miwmiexp⁡(βθ⋅Rθm+νθm)](9.5.5.11)\begin{bmatrix}\gamma^i\\ \theta^i\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\exp\left(\beta_\gamma\cdot R_\gamma^i+\nu_\gamma^i\right)\\ \frac{1}{P^A_{2017}}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}^i}w_m^i\exp\left(\beta_\theta\cdot R_\theta^m+\nu_\theta^m\right)\end{bmatrix} \tag{9.5.5.11}[γiθi​]=[exp(βγ​⋅Rγi​+νγi​)P2017A​1​∑m∈Mi​wmi​exp(βθ​⋅Rθm​+νθm​)​](9.5.5.11)

The regressands are log CO2_22​e per hectare of primary forest (site level) and log value of cattle sold for slaughter per hectare of pasture (municipality level); RγiR_\gamma^iRγi​ and RθmR_\theta^mRθm​ are geographic regressors and the ν\nuν's are random effects, common within each of the 78 coarse sites for γ\gammaγ and within each Amazonian water basin for θ\thetaθ. Collecting regression coefficients, random effects, regression-error precisions η\etaη and random-effect precisions ζ\zetaζ:

ρ′=(βγ′,νγ′,ηγ,ζγ,βθ′,νθ′,ηθ,ζθ),φ=Φ(ρ)(9.5.5.12)\rho'=\left(\beta_\gamma',\nu_\gamma',\eta_\gamma,\zeta_\gamma,\beta_\theta',\nu_\theta',\eta_\theta,\zeta_\theta\right),\qquad \varphi=\Phi(\rho) \tag{9.5.5.12}ρ′=(βγ′​,νγ′​,ηγ​,ζγ​,βθ′​,νθ′​,ηθ​,ζθ​),φ=Φ(ρ)(9.5.5.12)

The dimension of ρ\rhoρ is much smaller than 2×I2\times I2×I, which is key for computation. With baseline posterior π^\hat{\pi}π^ over ρ\rhoρ, the planner tilts densities g^(ρ)\hat{g}(\rho)g^​(ρ) directly in ρ\rhoρ-space and evaluates f[d,Φ(ρ)]f[d,\Phi(\rho)]f[d,Φ(ρ)]. The inner minimization has the familiar exponential tilting solution:

g^∗(ρ)=exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])∫exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)(9.5.5.13)\hat{g}^*(\rho)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)}{\int\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho)} \tag{9.5.5.13}g^​∗(ρ)=∫exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])​(9.5.5.13)

which puts more weight on parameter values with low discounted utility, and the minimized objective is:

−ξlog⁡∫exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)(9.5.5.14)-\xi\log\int\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho) \tag{9.5.5.14}−ξlog∫exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)(9.5.5.14)

This is a special case of both variational preferences and the smooth ambiguity model of Klibanoff, Marinacci and Mukerji (2005), but derived from distributional robustness rather than axioms. As ξ→∞\xi\to\inftyξ→∞ it collapses to expected utility under π^\hat{\pi}π^. By the min-max theorem the order of max and min can be exchanged (Problem 4.2), so the robust decision is optimal against a worst-case probability; inspecting these worst-case distributions is used to judge the plausibility of ξ\xiξ and to reveal which measurement uncertainties matter most for decisions.

Data and Parameter Estimation

Sites and initial states. MapBiomas 30 m pixels are aggregated to 1,887 sites; dropping those with less than 3% overlap with the biome leaves 1,043 sites. A coarser grid of 130 sites gives 78 sites. zˉi\bar{z}^izˉi and Z0iZ_0^iZ0i​ come from the shares of pixels classified as agriculture plus forest, and agriculture, in 2017.

Carbon density. From a random sample of 1.2 million pixels, 893,753 pixels with no deforestation in 1985–2017 are treated as primary forest and matched to ESA Biomass CCI 2017 above-ground biomass; biomass is halved to get carbon and multiplied by 44/12 to get CO2_22​e. The γ\gammaγ regression (1,043 sites, random effects by the 78 coarse sites) uses log precipitation, log temperature, latitude, longitude and their interaction.

Cattle productivity. The 2017 Agricultural Census gives the value of cattle sold for slaughter per hectare of pasture for 466 of the 540 municipalities intersecting the biome; the regression fills in the rest. Regressors are historical precipitation, temperature and its square, latitude and its square, log farm-gate cattle price (proxying unobserved transport costs) and distance to the state capital, with random effects for 70 basin groups and pasture-area weights. In generic form, each regression is:

Y=Rβ+Zν+ϵ,ϵ∼Normal(0,1ηΣ),[βν]∣ η,ζ∼Normal([00],[1ηΩ−1001ζI])(9.5.5.15)Y=R\beta+\mathcal{Z}\nu+\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\text{Normal}\left(0,\tfrac{1}{\eta}\Sigma\right),\qquad \begin{bmatrix}\beta\\ \nu\end{bmatrix}\Big|\,\eta,\zeta\sim\text{Normal}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\eta}\Omega^{-1}&0\\ 0&\frac{1}{\zeta}I\end{bmatrix}\right) \tag{9.5.5.15}Y=Rβ+Zν+ϵ,ϵ∼Normal(0,η1​Σ),[βν​]​η,ζ∼Normal([00​],[η1​Ω−10​0ζ1​I​])(9.5.5.15)

with Z\mathcal{Z}Z the group-indicator matrix, Σ\SigmaΣ a prespecified diagonal matrix and improper gamma priors on the precisions (a conditional normal/inverse-gamma setup). The fit is better for γ\gammaγ than for θ\thetaθ. Estimated γi\gamma^iγi ranges roughly from 200 to 1,100 Mg CO2_22​e/ha and θi\theta^iθi from 0.1 to 5; their correlation across the 1,043 sites is −0.27-0.27−0.27, so good pasture and dense forest are only imperfectly substitutable locations.

Validating regrowth. 21.3 million hectares of 120 m pixels classified as secondary vegetation in 2017 provide a natural experiment. The ratio of observed carbon to its model maximum is regressed on forest-age dummies (age is MapBiomas age plus five years):

Xpzˉpγp=∑tβt 1{t(p)=t}+ϵp(9.5.5.16)\frac{X_p}{\bar{z}_p\gamma_p}=\sum_{t}\beta_t\,\mathbb{1}\{t(p)=t\}+\epsilon_p \tag{9.5.5.16}zˉp​γp​Xp​​=t∑​βt​1{t(p)=t}+ϵp​(9.5.5.16)

(R2=0.66R^2=0.66R2=0.66). The empirical recovery curve lies above 1−e−αt1-e^{-\alpha t}1−e−αt, so the assumed regrowth is not overly optimistic and, if anything, understates sequestration by young forests.

Other parameters. κ=2.0942\kappa=2.0942κ=2.0942 is the area-weighted average of agricultural net emissions (SEEG) per hectare of agricultural area across Amazon states, 1990–2019. δ=0.02\delta=0.02δ=0.02. ζ1\zeta_1ζ1​ is calibrated so that the model's average marginal cost of deforestation (using 2008–2017 clearing) matches the price gap between forested and cleared land; ζ2\zeta_2ζ2​ so that the marginal cost of natural regeneration matches reforestation cost estimates. Monthly deflated cattle prices from 1995 to 2017 are fit with a two-state hidden Markov model with Gaussian noise: prices Pa=35.7P^a=35.7Pa=35.7 and 44.344.344.3, annual probabilities of staying of 0.710.710.71 (low) and 0.830.830.83 (high), and stationary mean 41.141.141.1.

Solution Method

Deterministic, ambiguity-neutral case. With the cattle price fixed at its stationary mean and productivities at their baseline means, the planner's problem over 1,043 sites is solved as one large static optimization over all trajectories for 200 years, discretized in annual steps:

Xt+1i=Xti−γiUti−α[Xti−γi(zˉi−Zti)],Zt+1i=Zti+Uti−Vti(9.5.5.17)X_{t+1}^i=X_t^i-\gamma^iU_t^i-\alpha\left[X_t^i-\gamma^i\left(\bar{z}^i-Z_t^i\right)\right],\qquad Z_{t+1}^i=Z_t^i+U_t^i-V_t^i \tag{9.5.5.17}Xt+1i​=Xti​−γiUti​−α[Xti​−γi(zˉi−Zti​)],Zt+1i​=Zti​+Uti​−Vti​(9.5.5.17)

Many state constraints bind at the optimum (corner solutions are common given the heterogeneity), so an interior point method with log-barrier penalties on nonnegative variables is used.

Ambiguity aversion. The robust problem is solved by iterating between maximization and minimization: given the worst-case mean productivities φˉs\bar{\varphi}_sφˉ​s​, solve for d(s)d^{(s)}d(s); given d(s)d^{(s)}d(s), compute the tilted distribution over ρ\rhoρ and its mean φ~s\tilde{\varphi}_sφ~​s​; update φˉs+1=0.75φˉs+0.25φ~s\bar{\varphi}_{s+1}=0.75\bar{\varphi}_s+0.25\tilde{\varphi}_sφˉ​s+1​=0.75φˉ​s​+0.25φ~​s​ until the sup-norm change is below 0.005. The tilted distribution is sampled by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan, NUTS) by treating −f/ξ-f/\xi−f/ξ as an extra log-likelihood term, i.e. using the potential energy:

U(ρ)=1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)]−log⁡L(Y ∣ R,Z,ρ)−log⁡π(ρ)(9.5.5.18)\mathcal{U}(\rho)=\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]-\log L\left(Y\,|\,R,\mathcal{Z},\rho\right)-\log\pi(\rho) \tag{9.5.5.18}U(ρ)=ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)]−logL(Y∣R,Z,ρ)−logπ(ρ)(9.5.5.18)

Each round uses 4 chains of 1,000 draws after 500 burn-in draws; a final sample has 16,000 draws.

Stochastic prices. With price randomness, recursive HJB methods are infeasible given the heterogeneity and state constraints, so the paper uses model predictive control (MPC) on the 78-site grid. From each date, the future is split into an uncertainty horizon of τ\tauτ periods, over which controls are measurable functions of realized prices (the scenario tree grows geometrically in τ\tauτ), and the remaining periods, in which the price is frozen at its date-τ\tauτ value. The first-period decision is implemented, the state is updated, and the problem is re-solved. Comparing V(τ)−V(τ−1)V(\tau)-V(\tau-1)V(τ)−V(τ−1) gives τ∗=3\tau^*=3τ∗=3.

Robustness to price dynamics. The paper also allows for misspecified transition probabilities, penalized period by period with parameter ξ^\hat{\xi}ξ^​ (following Anderson, Hansen and Sargent (2003)), distinct from ξ\xiξ for productivities. Over the MPC uncertainty horizon of length hhh, values along each price history kkk are built backward with a discrete-time exponential tilting recursion:

Ct+1,h−ℓ(k−ℓ)=[1−e−δ]ut+1,h−ℓ(k−ℓ)−e−δξ^log⁡∑j=1nπkh−ℓ,jexp⁡[−1ξ^Ct+1,h−ℓ+1(k−ℓ,j)](9.5.5.19)C_{t+1,h-\ell}(k_{-\ell})=\left[1-e^{-\delta}\right]u_{t+1,h-\ell}(k_{-\ell})-e^{-\delta}\hat{\xi}\log\sum_{j=1}^{n}\pi_{k_{h-\ell},j}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{\hat{\xi}}C_{t+1,h-\ell+1}(k_{-\ell},j)\right] \tag{9.5.5.19}Ct+1,h−ℓ​(k−ℓ​)=[1−e−δ]ut+1,h−ℓ​(k−ℓ​)−e−δξ^​logj=1∑n​πkh−ℓ​,j​exp[−ξ^​1​Ct+1,h−ℓ+1​(k−ℓ​,j)](9.5.5.19)

starting from deterministic terminal values. Because the distortion can differ every period, there is no learning, and the robustness concerns are about model misspecification rather than parameter uncertainty.

Business-as-Usual Shadow Price

The shadow price PeeP^{ee}Pee is backed out by taking the observed state (Xt‾o,Zt‾o)(X^o_{\underline{t}},Z^o_{\underline{t}})(Xt​o​,Zt​o​) in t‾=1995\underline{t}=1995t​=1995 (first year of reliable post-stabilization price data), feeding in the realized cattle price path, and choosing a time-invariant PeeP^{ee}Pee so that predicted aggregate deforestation through tˉ=2008\bar{t}=2008tˉ=2008 (start of the Amazon Fund) matches the data:

∑i=1I(Ztˉi−Zt‾i)∣Pe=Pee=observed deforestation over [t‾,tˉ](9.5.5.20)\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(Z_{\bar{t}}^i-Z_{\underline{t}}^i\right)\Big|_{P^e=P^{ee}}=\text{observed deforestation over }[\underline{t},\bar{t}] \tag{9.5.5.20}i=1∑I​(Ztˉi​−Zt​i​)​Pe=Pee​=observed deforestation over [t​,tˉ](9.5.5.20)

With 1,043 sites and a constant price of 41.1, Pee=6.8P^{ee}=6.8Pee=6.8 dollars per ton under ambiguity neutrality, and it falls with ambiguity aversion: 5.6 (ξ=2\xi=2ξ=2), 4.8 (ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1) and 2.8 (ξ=0.5\xi=0.5ξ=0.5). Ambiguity about productivity slows the destruction of near-virgin forest, so a lower implied shadow price is needed to rationalize the same history. With 78 sites the price is 6.7, and under stochastic prices it is 6.9, 6.5 and 6.1 for ξ^=∞,1,0.5\hat{\xi}=\infty,1,0.5ξ^​=∞,1,0.5. Forward simulations start in 2017 and report results by bbb, which ties directly to transfer payments; because PeeP^{ee}Pee adjusts, quantity paths for a given bbb are fairly insensitive to specification and to raising δ\deltaδ from two to three percent.

Key Results

  • Business as usual. With Pe=Pee=6.8P^e=P^{ee}=6.8Pe=Pee=6.8 and no transfers, agricultural area rises from 15% to about 20% of the biome over 30 years, a level that Lovejoy and Nobre (2018) and Flores et al. (2024) associate with possible tipping-point loss of the rainforest. Net emissions are about 12.1 Gt CO2_22​e over 15 years and 14.7 Gt over 30 years.

  • Transfers trigger large-scale restoration. With b=15b=15b=15 or 252525, pasture shrinks sharply, much of it within the first 15 years, and cattle survive only in a small southern and eastern fringe. With b=15b=15b=15, net capture is 8.8 Gt by year 15 and 16.3 Gt by year 30; with b=25b=25b=25, 10.3 and 17.8 Gt. Transfer flows peak after about 10 years and then decline as forests mature.

  • Present values (200 years, ambiguity neutral). At b=0b=0b=0 the planner value is 261 billion dollars (cattle 376, forest services −108-108−108, adjustment costs 6). At b=25b=25b=25 it is 525 billion: cattle output falls by 360 billion (to 16), more than offset by 417 billion in transfers and 221 billion of additional forest services valued at PeeP^{ee}Pee, a net gain of 264 billion. Even b=10b=10b=10 more than compensates the loss of cattle income.

  • Effective cost. Defined as discounted net transfers divided by the additional net capture relative to b=0b=0b=0, the effective cost per ton is far below bbb: 3.6 and 4.8 dollars (15 and 30 years) at b=10b=10b=10, 6.3 and 7.9 at b=15b=15b=15, and 11.5 and 13.7 at b=25b=25b=25, because transfers also buy avoided business-as-usual deforestation. At b=25b=25b=25 emissions fall by about 22 Gt CO2_22​e in 15 years and 32 Gt in 30 years relative to business as usual, about 10% of the global nature-based potential estimated by Griscom et al. (2017).

  • Ambiguity aversion. At b=0b=0b=0, worst-case tilts are much larger for agricultural productivities θ\thetaθ; at b=15b=15b=15, when reforestation becomes the main objective, they shift to carbon densities γ\gammaγ. Holding Pee=6.8P^{ee}=6.8Pee=6.8 fixed, ambiguity aversion delays deforestation and keeps agricultural area roughly flat instead of rising toward 20%. Once PeeP^{ee}Pee adjusts endogenously to 4.8, this effect disappears (agricultural area even ends somewhat higher), and at b=15b=15b=15 land paths under ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1 and ξ=∞\xi=\inftyξ=∞ are nearly identical. Planner values fall by 27% at b=0b=0b=0 and 8% at b=25b=25b=25, so the percentage gain from moving to b=25b=25b=25 is larger under ambiguity aversion.

  • Price risk. Stochastic cattle prices barely change aggregate paths relative to the constant-price case. Misspecification aversion pushes the worst-case probability of staying in the low price state from 0.71 to 0.91 (ξ^=1\hat{\xi}=1ξ^​=1) and 0.98 (ξ^=0.5\hat{\xi}=0.5ξ^​=0.5), and lowers the probability of staying high from 0.83 to 0.52 and 0.16, lowering the business-as-usual planner value from 239 to 221 and 209 billion. At b=15b=15b=15 the distortions are small (0.72/0.81 and 0.74/0.80) and values barely move.

Extensions: Time Consistency and a Conservation Fund

The plan is optimal under commitment at date zero, but as restored forests mature, sequestration and payments fall and Brazil may want to re-deforest. The paper proposes a conservation fund held by a third party: per net ton captured Brazil receives b‾\underline{b}b​ directly and bfb_fbf​ is deposited in a fund earning interest δ\deltaδ, with b=b‾+bfb=\underline{b}+b_fb=b​+bf​. Before the threshold date τf\tau_fτf​ interest accumulates; afterwards it is paid to Brazil. The balance evolves as:

B˙t={δBt+bf∑i=1I(X˙ti−κZti)if t<τfbf∑i=1I(X˙ti−κZti)if t≥τf(9.5.5.21)\dot{B}_t=\begin{cases}\delta B_t+b_f\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\dot{X}_t^i-\kappa Z_t^i\right) & \text{if } t<\tau_f\\ b_f\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\dot{X}_t^i-\kappa Z_t^i\right) & \text{if } t\ge\tau_f\end{cases} \tag{9.5.5.21}B˙t​=⎩⎨⎧​δBt​+bf​∑i=1I​(X˙ti​−κZti​)bf​∑i=1I​(X˙ti​−κZti​)​if t<τf​if t≥τf​​(9.5.5.21)

If net reforestation falls short of the plan (verified on land allocation rather than carbon, to insulate Brazil from carbon shocks beyond its control), payments stop and the fund is forfeited. With V(X,Z,b)V(X,Z,b)V(X,Z,b) the value of stocks (X,Z)(X,Z)(X,Z) under transfers bbb going forward and P^a\hat{P}^aP^a the constant cattle price, a deviation at ttt occurs only if:

eδt∫t∞e−δs[P^a∑i=1IAsi−(Pee+b)∑i=1I(κZsi−X˙si)−LCs]ds<V(Xt,Zt,0)−Bt(9.5.5.22)e^{\delta t}\int_t^\infty e^{-\delta s}\left[\hat{P}^a\sum_{i=1}^{I}A_s^i-\left(P^{ee}+b\right)\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_s^i-\dot{X}_s^i\right)-LC_s\right]ds<V\left(X_t,Z_t,0\right)-B_t \tag{9.5.5.22}eδt∫t∞​e−δs[P^ai=1∑I​Asi​−(Pee+b)i=1∑I​(κZsi​−X˙si​)−LCs​]ds<V(Xt​,Zt​,0)−Bt​(9.5.5.22)

With b=25b=25b=25, bf=0.15bb_f=0.15bbf​=0.15b and τf=15\tau_f=15τf​=15 years there is no defection within 100 years; τf=21\tau_f=21τf​=21 rules it out permanently; bf=0.2bb_f=0.2bbf​=0.2b works even with τf=0\tau_f=0τf​=0. A modest escrowed share therefore suffices, in contrast to fully funding the fund up front (Scheinkman (2024)) or treating payments as loans (Harstad (2025)). Omitted from the model: effects of deforestation on rainfall and agricultural productivity, biodiversity and tipping points, cross-site spillovers, and real-time learning about productivities.

This is the production technology for cattle: output AtiA_t^iAti​ of site iii is linear in pasture area ZtiZ_t^iZti​ with a site-specific and time-invariant yield θi\theta^iθi. The value of output is PtaAti=PtaθiZtiP_t^aA_t^i=P_t^a\theta^iZ_t^iPta​Ati​=Pta​θiZti​, where PtaP_t^aPta​ is a national price index, so θi\theta^iθi is measured in units such that P2017AθiP^A_{2017}\theta^iP2017A​θi equals the 2017 value of cattle sold for slaughter per hectare of pasture in the site (see equation (11)); it therefore also absorbs the ratio of local farm-gate to national prices, i.e. transport costs.

Linearity means constant returns to land within a site: there is no intensive margin (stocking rates, pasture improvement), no other inputs, and no decline of yields as worse land within the site is cleared. Heterogeneity in land quality is captured only across sites, through the distribution of θi\theta^iθi, which ranges from about 0.10.10.1 to 555. Because output is valued at revenue with no input costs, the marginal return to a hectare of pasture is

∂(PtaAti)∂Zti=Ptaθi\frac{\partial\left(P_t^aA_t^i\right)}{\partial Z_t^i}=P_t^a\theta^i∂Zti​∂(Pta​Ati​)​=Pta​θi

which overstates the net return and biases the model toward agriculture. With θi=1\theta^i=1θi=1 and Pa=41.1P^a=41.1Pa=41.1 a hectare yields about 414141 dollars per year, with present value 41.1/δ≈2,05541.1/\delta\approx 2{,}05541.1/δ≈2,055 dollars at δ=0.02\delta=0.02δ=0.02. A linear technology combined with the linear carbon dynamics makes the flow payoff in equation (8) linear in the states, so sites tend to go to corners Zi=0Z^i=0Zi=0 or Zi=zˉiZ^i=\bar{z}^iZi=zˉi, with the speed of transition governed by the adjustment costs of equation (7).

This is an accounting definition of the net emissions flow of the whole biome, in Mg CO2_22​e per year. The first term is the emissions of the agricultural activity itself: κ\kappaκ (calibrated to about 2.092.092.09 Mg CO2_22​e per hectare per year) times total pasture area, mainly enteric fermentation and soil management. The second term is minus the change in the carbon stored in forests: when X˙ti<0\dot{X}_t^i<0X˙ti​<0 carbon leaves the forest and enters the atmosphere, and when X˙ti>0\dot{X}_t^i>0X˙ti​>0 regrowing forest absorbs carbon and net emissions fall. A negative value of the whole expression is net capture, which is what international transfers pay for.

Substituting the carbon law of motion, equation (3), shows the three sources separately:

Net emissionst=∑i=1I{κZti+γiUti−α[γi(zˉi−Zti)−Xti]}\text{Net emissions}_t=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left\{\kappa Z_t^i+\gamma^iU_t^i-\alpha\left[\gamma^i\left(\bar{z}^i-Z_t^i\right)-X_t^i\right]\right\}Net emissionst​=i=1∑I​{κZti​+γiUti​−α[γi(zˉi−Zti​)−Xti​]}

namely cattle emissions, the instantaneous release from clearing, and sequestration proportional to the remaining carbon gap of regrowing forest. Cumulated over time, the forest part equals the change in the stock, −∫0t∑iX˙si ds=∑i(X0i−Xti)-\int_0^t\sum_i\dot{X}_s^i\,ds=\sum_i\left(X_0^i-X_t^i\right)−∫0t​∑i​X˙si​ds=∑i​(X0i​−Xti​), so only cattle emissions keep accumulating in a steady state. Net emissions are priced at PeP^ePe in the objective of equation (8), and their negative is the base of the transfer in equation (9) and of the deposits into the conservation fund in equation (21). The definition treats a ton emitted and a ton captured symmetrically and ignores other greenhouse or climate effects of the forest.

This is the assumed cost of changing land use, in dollars per year. The two controls enter through their totals over all sites: ∑iUti\sum_iU_t^i∑i​Uti​ is hectares cleared per year in the whole biome and ∑iVti\sum_iV_t^i∑i​Vti​ is hectares put into regeneration; ζ1\zeta_1ζ1​ and ζ2\zeta_2ζ2​ are the corresponding cost parameters. The quadratic form gives marginal costs that are linear in aggregate activity and identical across sites:

∂LCt∂Uti=ζ1∑j=1IUtj,∂LCt∂Vti=ζ2∑j=1IVtj\frac{\partial LC_t}{\partial U_t^i}=\zeta_1\sum_{j=1}^{I}U_t^j,\qquad \frac{\partial LC_t}{\partial V_t^i}=\zeta_2\sum_{j=1}^{I}V_t^j∂Uti​∂LCt​​=ζ1​j=1∑I​Utj​,∂Vti​∂LCt​​=ζ2​j=1∑I​Vtj​

The interpretation is an upward-sloping supply of the resources needed to clear land or remove farms (labor, machinery, enforcement), which are mobile across the Amazon. These formulas are also what the calibration uses: ζ1\zeta_1ζ1​ is set so that the marginal cost at observed 2008–2017 clearing equals the price gap between forested and cleared land, and ζ2\zeta_2ζ2​ so that the marginal cost of regeneration matches reforestation cost estimates.

Two implications follow. First, because marginal cost rises with the aggregate rate, transitions are spread out over time rather than happening instantly, even though the rest of the flow payoff in equation (8) is linear. Second, because the marginal cost is the same for every site, the planner ranks sites by their net benefit and converts the best ones first and fully; costs do not penalize concentrating all activity in one site, so there is no force toward small simultaneous changes everywhere. Separate terms for UUU and VVV (rather than a function of net change) mean that clearing in one site and regrowth in another both cost resources. This is the only explicit link across sites in the objective.

This defines the planner's payoff from a decision process ddd given the productivity vector φ=(γi,θi)i=1I\varphi=(\gamma^i,\theta^i)_{i=1}^Iφ=(γi,θi)i=1I​. A decision process is a full contingent plan for (Uti,Vti)(U_t^i,V_t^i)(Uti​,Vti​) as a function of the history of cattle prices. Inside the integral, the first term is the revenue from cattle, using equation (5); the second is net emissions from equation (6) valued at the emissions price PeP^ePe; the third is the land-use-change cost of equation (7). The flow is discounted at the subjective rate δ\deltaδ, and the expectation is over paths of the Markov chain PtaP_t^aPta​ of equation (1) only; it is conditional on φ\varphiφ, because uncertainty about φ\varphiφ is treated separately, with ambiguity aversion, in equation (10). The planner is risk neutral with respect to price risk.

The carbon term can be rewritten by integrating by parts (the stock is bounded, so the boundary term at infinity vanishes):

∫0∞e−δtX˙ti dt=−X0i+δ∫0∞e−δtXti dt\int_0^\infty e^{-\delta t}\dot{X}_t^i\,dt=-X_0^i+\delta\int_0^\infty e^{-\delta t}X_t^i\,dt∫0∞​e−δtX˙ti​dt=−X0i​+δ∫0∞​e−δtXti​dt

so paying PeP^ePe for each change in the stock is equivalent to paying a rental of δPe\delta P^eδPe per ton stored per year. This yields a simple static benchmark: keeping one hectare of mature forest forever is worth PeγiP^e\gamma^iPeγi in carbon, while keeping it as pasture is worth (Paθi−Peκ)/δ(P^a\theta^i-P^e\kappa)/\delta(Paθi−Peκ)/δ, so absent adjustment costs and regrowth dynamics the forest is preferred when

Pe(δγi+κ)>PaθiP^e\left(\delta\gamma^i+\kappa\right)>P^a\theta^iPe(δγi+κ)>Paθi

For example, γi=500\gamma^i=500γi=500, θi=1\theta^i=1θi=1, Pa=41.1P^a=41.1Pa=41.1 and δ=0.02\delta=0.02δ=0.02 give a break-even emissions price of about 41.1/12.1≈3.441.1/12.1\approx 3.441.1/12.1≈3.4 dollars per ton. The function fff is the building block of the robust problem in equation (10), the tilting formulas in equations (13)–(14) and the sampler in equation (18).

The decomposition follows from adding international transfers to Brazil's own objective. Without transfers, the planner values net emissions at its own shadow price PeeP^{ee}Pee, so its flow payoff is the bracket in equation (8) with PeP^ePe replaced by PeeP^{ee}Pee:

Pta∑i=1IAti−Pee∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)−LCtP_t^a\sum_{i=1}^{I}A_t^i-P^{ee}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)-LC_tPta​i=1∑I​Ati​−Peei=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)−LCt​

Under the transfer scheme Brazil receives bbb dollars per ton of net capture. Net capture is the negative of net emissions in equation (6), so the transfer flow is

b Et,Et:=∑i=1I(X˙ti−κZti)=−∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)b\,E_t,\qquad E_t:=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\dot{X}_t^i-\kappa Z_t^i\right)=-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)bEt​,Et​:=i=1∑I​(X˙ti​−κZti​)=−i=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)

Adding the transfer to the flow payoff and collecting the terms that multiply net emissions:

Pta∑i=1IAti−Pee∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)−b∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)−LCt=Pta∑i=1IAti−(Pee+b)∑i=1I(κZti−X˙ti)−LCt\begin{aligned} &P_t^a\sum_{i=1}^{I}A_t^i-P^{ee}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)-b\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)-LC_t\\ &\quad=P_t^a\sum_{i=1}^{I}A_t^i-\left(P^{ee}+b\right)\sum_{i=1}^{I}\left(\kappa Z_t^i-\dot{X}_t^i\right)-LC_t \end{aligned}​Pta​i=1∑I​Ati​−Peei=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)−bi=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)−LCt​=Pta​i=1∑I​Ati​−(Pee+b)i=1∑I​(κZti​−X˙ti​)−LCt​​

This is exactly the flow in equation (8) with Pe=Pee+bP^e=P^{ee}+bPe=Pee+b. Two remarks. The transfer is linear in EtE_tEt​ and applies also when Et<0E_t<0Et​<0: with net emissions Brazil in effect pays bbb per ton, which is why paying for net capture implicitly taxes deforestation, and why the planner's behaviour depends only on the sum Pee+bP^{ee}+bPee+b. The split still matters for accounting: the value in equation (8) evaluated at PeP^ePe mixes actual cash, b∫e−δtEt dtb\int e^{-\delta t}E_t\,dtb∫e−δtEt​dt, with Brazil's own non-cash valuation of forest services at PeeP^{ee}Pee, which the note reports separately.

This is the robust planner's problem. The outer player chooses the contingent land-use plan ddd from the feasible set D\mathcal{D}D. The inner, fictitious player chooses a density ggg of an alternative distribution of productivities relative to the baseline π\piπ (so g dπg\,d\pigdπ is a probability measure, hence g≥0g\ge 0g≥0 and ∫g dπ=1\int g\,d\pi=1∫gdπ=1) to make the planner's expected payoff ∫f g dπ\int f\,g\,d\pi∫fgdπ small. The second term is ξ\xiξ times the relative entropy of the alternative with respect to the baseline,

∫glog⁡g dπ ≥ (∫g dπ)log⁡(∫g dπ)=0\int g\log g\,d\pi\ \ge\ \left(\int g\,d\pi\right)\log\left(\int g\,d\pi\right)=0∫gloggdπ ≥ (∫gdπ)log(∫gdπ)=0

where the inequality is Jensen's inequality for the convex function xlog⁡xx\log xxlogx, with equality only at g=1g=1g=1. The penalty therefore makes it costly for the minimizing player to move far from π\piπ, and ξ>0\xi>0ξ>0 is the price of doing so, in the same dollar units as fff. As ξ→∞\xi\to\inftyξ→∞ any departure is infinitely costly, the minimizer picks g=1g=1g=1, and the problem reduces to maximizing ∫f dπ\int f\,d\pi∫fdπ (ambiguity neutrality). As ξ\xiξ falls, the planner guards against a wider set of distributions.

Why this form: the inner problem has the closed-form solution in equations (13) and (14), so ambiguity aversion only replaces the expectation by a log-exponential certainty equivalent; the objective is linear in ggg plus a strictly convex penalty, so the minimizer is unique and the order of max and min can be exchanged. What it rules out: learning, since ggg is chosen once at date zero, and alternatives that are not absolutely continuous with respect to π\piπ. In the implementation the distortion is applied to the low-dimensional regression parameters ρ\rhoρ of equation (12) rather than to φ\varphiφ directly. The parameter ξ\xiξ is not estimated; it is judged by inspecting the implied worst-case distributions.

This maps the two measurement regressions into the model productivities of site iii. The first row says that log carbon density of primary forest is a linear index of site-level geographic regressors RγiR_\gamma^iRγi​ (log precipitation, log temperature, latitude, longitude and their interaction) plus a random effect νγi\nu_\gamma^iνγi​ shared by all fine sites inside the same coarse site; exponentiating gives γi>0\gamma^i>0γi>0 in Mg CO2_22​e per hectare. The second row is built from a municipality-level regression: exp⁡(βθ⋅Rθm+νθm)\exp(\beta_\theta\cdot R_\theta^m+\nu_\theta^m)exp(βθ​⋅Rθm​+νθm​) is the predicted 2017 value of cattle sold for slaughter per hectare of pasture in municipality mmm (with a basin-level random effect), these predictions are averaged over the municipalities Mi\mathcal{M}^iMi that intersect the site with area weights wmiw_m^iwmi​ summing to one, and the result is divided by the 2017 cattle price so that PtaθiP_t^a\theta^iPta​θi is a value per hectare at any date, consistent with equation (5).

The log-linear form guarantees positive productivities and makes regressors act proportionally. Note that the idiosyncratic regression errors ϵ\epsilonϵ of equation (15) are not included: γi\gamma^iγi and θi\theta^iθi are the systematic (fitted plus random-effect) components, so the only uncertainty about them is uncertainty about (β,ν)(\beta,\nu)(β,ν). A special case shows the units: if a site lies in a single municipality with predicted value VmV_mVm​ dollars per hectare, then

θi=VmP2017A,PtaθiZti=PtaP2017A VmZti\theta^i=\frac{V_m}{P^A_{2017}},\qquad P_t^a\theta^iZ_t^i=\frac{P_t^a}{P^A_{2017}}\,V_mZ_t^iθi=P2017A​Vm​​,Pta​θiZti​=P2017A​Pta​​Vm​Zti​

i.e. 2017 revenue scaled by the price index. The coefficients are identified from cross-sectional variation in biomass across primary-forest pixels and in census cattle revenue across the 466 municipalities with data. The map is the function Φ\PhiΦ of equation (12).

The vector ρ\rhoρ stacks everything that is uncertain in the two regressions of equation (15): for carbon density, the coefficients βγ\beta_\gammaβγ​, the vector of random effects νγ\nu_\gammaνγ​ (one per coarse site), the precision of the regression error ηγ\eta_\gammaηγ​ and the precision of the random effects ζγ\zeta_\gammaζγ​; and the same four objects for cattle productivity, with random effects by water-basin group. The function Φ\PhiΦ is equation (11) applied to every site, so it returns the full vector φ\varphiφ of length 2I2I2I. Only β\betaβ and ν\nuν actually enter Φ\PhiΦ; the precisions matter because they shape the joint posterior π^\hat{\pi}π^ of ρ\rhoρ.

The point of the reparameterization is dimension. With I=1,043I=1{,}043I=1,043 sites, φ\varphiφ has 2,0862{,}0862,086 elements, while ρ\rhoρ has on the order of 170 (a handful of regression coefficients, 78 plus 70 random effects, four precisions). All uncertainty about φ\varphiφ is generated by uncertainty about ρ\rhoρ, so productivities of sites that share regressors or random effects are strongly dependent, and a distribution over φ\varphiφ is the image of a distribution over ρ\rhoρ. The robust problem of equation (10) is therefore posed over densities g^(ρ)\hat{g}(\rho)g^​(ρ) relative to π^\hat{\pi}π^:

max⁡d∈D min⁡g^≥0, ∫g^ dπ^=1 ∫f[d,Φ(ρ)]g^(ρ) dπ^(ρ)+ξ∫g^(ρ)log⁡g^(ρ) dπ^(ρ)\max_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\ \min_{\hat{g}\ge 0,\ \int\hat{g}\,d\hat{\pi}=1}\ \int f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\hat{g}(\rho)\,d\hat{\pi}(\rho)+\xi\int\hat{g}(\rho)\log\hat{g}(\rho)\,d\hat{\pi}(\rho)d∈Dmax​ g^​≥0, ∫g^​dπ^=1min​ ∫f[d,Φ(ρ)]g^​(ρ)dπ^(ρ)+ξ∫g^​(ρ)logg^​(ρ)dπ^(ρ)

This restricts the adversary to distortions that respect the regression structure (it can shift coefficients or a region's random effect, not each site independently) and makes sampling from the worst case feasible with the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo scheme of equation (18). The solutions are equations (13) and (14).

Fix the decision ddd and abbreviate f(ρ):=f[d,Φ(ρ)]f(\rho):=f[d,\Phi(\rho)]f(ρ):=f[d,Φ(ρ)]. The inner problem of equation (10), written in ρ\rhoρ-space as in equation (12), is

min⁡g^≥0 ∫f(ρ)g^(ρ) dπ^(ρ)+ξ∫g^(ρ)log⁡g^(ρ) dπ^(ρ)s.t.∫g^(ρ) dπ^(ρ)=1\min_{\hat{g}\ge 0}\ \int f(\rho)\hat{g}(\rho)\,d\hat{\pi}(\rho)+\xi\int\hat{g}(\rho)\log\hat{g}(\rho)\,d\hat{\pi}(\rho)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\int\hat{g}(\rho)\,d\hat{\pi}(\rho)=1g^​≥0min​ ∫f(ρ)g^​(ρ)dπ^(ρ)+ξ∫g^​(ρ)logg^​(ρ)dπ^(ρ)s.t.∫g^​(ρ)dπ^(ρ)=1

The objective is strictly convex in g^\hat{g}g^​ (linear term plus ξ\xiξ times the strictly convex xlog⁡xx\log xxlogx), so first-order conditions are sufficient. Attach a multiplier λ\lambdaλ to the adding-up constraint and form the Lagrangian

L=∫[f(ρ)g^(ρ)+ξg^(ρ)log⁡g^(ρ)+λg^(ρ)]dπ^(ρ)−λ\mathcal{L}=\int\left[f(\rho)\hat{g}(\rho)+\xi\hat{g}(\rho)\log\hat{g}(\rho)+\lambda\hat{g}(\rho)\right]d\hat{\pi}(\rho)-\lambdaL=∫[f(ρ)g^​(ρ)+ξg^​(ρ)logg^​(ρ)+λg^​(ρ)]dπ^(ρ)−λ

Minimize pointwise in g^(ρ)\hat{g}(\rho)g^​(ρ); the derivative of xlog⁡xx\log xxlogx is log⁡x+1\log x+1logx+1:

f(ρ)+ξ[log⁡g^(ρ)+1]+λ=0f(\rho)+\xi\left[\log\hat{g}(\rho)+1\right]+\lambda=0f(ρ)+ξ[logg^​(ρ)+1]+λ=0

Solve for the density. The nonnegativity constraint never binds because the solution is strictly positive (the slope of xlog⁡xx\log xxlogx is −∞-\infty−∞ at zero):

g^(ρ)=exp⁡(−1−λξ)exp⁡(−1ξf(ρ))\hat{g}(\rho)=\exp\left(-1-\frac{\lambda}{\xi}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f(\rho)\right)g^​(ρ)=exp(−1−ξλ​)exp(−ξ1​f(ρ))

The first factor is a constant, pinned down by integrating both sides against π^\hat{\pi}π^ and imposing the constraint:

exp⁡(−1−λξ)=[∫exp⁡(−1ξf(ρ))dπ^(ρ)]−1\exp\left(-1-\frac{\lambda}{\xi}\right)=\left[\int\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f(\rho)\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho)\right]^{-1}exp(−1−ξλ​)=[∫exp(−ξ1​f(ρ))dπ^(ρ)]−1

Substituting back gives the exponentially tilted density

g^∗(ρ)=exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])∫exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)\hat{g}^*(\rho)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)}{\int\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho)}g^​∗(ρ)=∫exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])​

The worst case reweights the baseline posterior toward parameter values where the chosen plan performs badly; the ratio of weights of two parameter values is exp⁡{−[f(ρ1)−f(ρ2)]/ξ}\exp\{-[f(\rho_1)-f(\rho_2)]/\xi\}exp{−[f(ρ1​)−f(ρ2​)]/ξ}, so a smaller ξ\xiξ means a stronger tilt and ξ→∞\xi\to\inftyξ→∞ gives g^∗=1\hat{g}^*=1g^​∗=1. The density depends on ddd: under business as usual the plan's payoff is most sensitive to θ\thetaθ, and under large transfers to γ\gammaγ, which is why the tilts move from one to the other.

Substitute the minimizer from equation (13) into the inner objective. Write f(ρ):=f[d,Φ(ρ)]f(\rho):=f[d,\Phi(\rho)]f(ρ):=f[d,Φ(ρ)] and K:=∫exp⁡(−f(ρ)/ξ)dπ^(ρ)K:=\int\exp\left(-f(\rho)/\xi\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho)K:=∫exp(−f(ρ)/ξ)dπ^(ρ), so that equation (13) reads g^∗=exp⁡(−f/ξ)/K\hat{g}^*=\exp(-f/\xi)/Kg^​∗=exp(−f/ξ)/K and

log⁡g^∗(ρ)=−1ξf(ρ)−log⁡K\log\hat{g}^*(\rho)=-\frac{1}{\xi}f(\rho)-\log Klogg^​∗(ρ)=−ξ1​f(ρ)−logK

using ∫g^∗dπ^=1\int\hat{g}^*d\hat{\pi}=1∫g^​∗dπ^=1 in the last line. Hence the value of the inner minimization is

−ξlog⁡∫exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)-\xi\log\int\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)d\hat{\pi}(\rho)−ξlog∫exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])dπ^(ρ)

and the robust planner simply maximizes this expression over ddd. It is a certainty equivalent of fff under the baseline posterior with an exponential (constant absolute aversion) transformation. To see how it relates to expected utility, expand in 1/ξ1/\xi1/ξ using the cumulant expansion log⁡E[esf]=s E[f]+s22Var⁡(f)+O(s3)\log\mathbb{E}\left[e^{sf}\right]=s\,\mathbb{E}[f]+\tfrac{s^2}{2}\operatorname{Var}(f)+O(s^3)logE[esf]=sE[f]+2s2​Var(f)+O(s3) with s=−1/ξs=-1/\xis=−1/ξ:

−ξlog⁡Eπ^[e−f/ξ]=Eπ^[f]−12ξVar⁡π^(f)+O(ξ−2)-\xi\log\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\pi}}\left[e^{-f/\xi}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\pi}}[f]-\frac{1}{2\xi}\operatorname{Var}_{\hat{\pi}}(f)+O\left(\xi^{-2}\right)−ξlogEπ^​[e−f/ξ]=Eπ^​[f]−2ξ1​Varπ^​(f)+O(ξ−2)

So as ξ→∞\xi\to\inftyξ→∞ the objective collapses to the posterior mean of fff, and for finite ξ\xiξ the planner pays a penalty for plans whose payoff is sensitive to the uncertain productivities. By Jensen's inequality the expression is never above Eπ^[f]\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\pi}}[f]Eπ^​[f] and it is increasing in ξ\xiξ, consistent with planner values that fall as ambiguity aversion rises.

This is the common statistical model behind both productivity regressions. YYY is the vector of log outcomes (log CO2_22​e per hectare by site, or log cattle value per hectare by municipality), RRR the matrix of geographic regressors with coefficients β\betaβ, and Z\mathcal{Z}Z a matrix of zeros and ones assigning each observation to its group (coarse site or basin group), so Zν\mathcal{Z}\nuZν adds a group-specific intercept ν\nuν. The error has variance Σ/η\Sigma/\etaΣ/η: η\etaη is a scalar precision and Σ\SigmaΣ a known diagonal matrix that allows observation weights (for cattle, pasture-area weights). The second part is the prior: conditional on the precisions, β\betaβ is normal with variance Ω−1/η\Omega^{-1}/\etaΩ−1/η, scaled by the error precision as in the conjugate normal-gamma setup, and the random effects are independent normal with common precision ζ\zetaζ, independent of β\betaβ. Improper gamma priors on η\etaη and ζ\zetaζ complete the hierarchy.

The structure buys tractability: conditional on (η,ζ)(\eta,\zeta)(η,ζ) the posterior of (β,ν)(\beta,\nu)(β,ν) is normal, and the full posterior π^\hat{\pi}π^ of the vector ρ\rhoρ in equation (12) is easy to sample. Economically, the random effects capture spatially correlated unobservables, and the prior shrinks them toward zero. In the simplest case with no regressors, Σ=I\Sigma=IΣ=I and ngn_gng​ observations with mean yˉg\bar{y}_gyˉ​g​ in group ggg, the posterior mean is

E[νg∣Y,η,ζ]=ηngηng+ζ yˉg\mathbb{E}\left[\nu_g\mid Y,\eta,\zeta\right]=\frac{\eta n_g}{\eta n_g+\zeta}\,\bar{y}_gE[νg​∣Y,η,ζ]=ηng​+ζηng​​yˉ​g​

so groups with few observations or noisy data are pulled more strongly toward the regression line. β\betaβ is identified from cross-sectional covariation of outcomes with geography, ν\nuν from within-group averages of residuals, and ζ\zetaζ from the dispersion of those averages. The posterior uncertainty about (β,ν)(\beta,\nu)(β,ν) is exactly the productivity uncertainty that the planner faces in equations (10)–(14) through the map in equation (11).

This regression is an external validity check of the regrowth assumption in equation (3), not an input to the model. The unit ppp is a 120 m pixel classified as secondary vegetation in 2017. XpX_pXp​ is its observed carbon, zˉpγp\bar{z}_p\gamma_pzˉp​γp​ is the model's ceiling for that pixel (area times the primary-forest density of its site), so the dependent variable is the share of mature carbon that has been recovered, a number between zero and one apart from measurement error. On the right is a full set of dummies for forest age t(p)t(p)t(p), so βt\beta_tβt​ is simply the average recovery ratio among pixels of age ttt, estimated nonparametrically with no functional form imposed across ages; ϵp\epsilon_pϵp​ is the within-age deviation.

The model counterpart follows from equation (4): a pixel that starts regrowing with no carbon has recovered a share

βtmodel=1−e−αt\beta_t^{\text{model}}=1-e^{-\alpha t}βtmodel​=1−e−αt

after ttt years, for instance 1−e−0.045×20≈0.591-e^{-0.045\times 20}\approx 0.591−e−0.045×20≈0.59 at age 20. Comparing the estimated βt\beta_tβt​ with this curve tests both the exponential shape and the level of α\alphaα. Identification is cross-sectional: pixels abandoned at different dates are compared in a single year, which requires that pixels of different ages are otherwise similar (normalizing by γp\gamma_pγp​ controls for location-specific carbon potential) and that age is measured correctly; the five years added to the MapBiomas age account for the lag before regrowth is classified as secondary vegetation. The finding that the estimated βt\beta_tβt​ lie above the model curve means the assumed dynamics understate early sequestration, so the model's gains from reforestation are conservative.

These are the continuous-time laws of motion, equations (2) and (3), discretized with an explicit Euler step of one year. Integrate equation (3) over [t,t+1][t,t+1][t,t+1]:

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samples from a density proportional to exp⁡[−U(ρ)]\exp[-\mathcal{U}(\rho)]exp[−U(ρ)], so the potential energy must be minus the log of the target density up to a constant. The target is the worst-case distribution of ρ\rhoρ. By equation (13) its density relative to the baseline posterior π^\hat{\pi}π^ is the exponential tilt, so with p^(ρ)\hat{p}(\rho)p^​(ρ) denoting the density of π^\hat{\pi}π^,

p∗(ρ)=g^∗(ρ) p^(ρ) ∝ exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])p^(ρ)p^*(\rho)=\hat{g}^*(\rho)\,\hat{p}(\rho)\ \propto\ \exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)\hat{p}(\rho)p∗(ρ)=g^​∗(ρ)p^​(ρ) ∝ exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])p^​(ρ)

The baseline posterior comes from the regressions of equation (15). By Bayes' rule it is proportional to the likelihood of the data times the prior density of ρ\rhoρ, which the note writes as π(ρ)\pi(\rho)π(ρ):

p^(ρ) ∝ L(Y∣R,Z,ρ)π(ρ)\hat{p}(\rho)\ \propto\ L\left(Y\mid R,\mathcal{Z},\rho\right)\pi(\rho)p^​(ρ) ∝ L(Y∣R,Z,ρ)π(ρ)

Combining the two lines,

p∗(ρ) ∝ exp⁡(−1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)])L(Y∣R,Z,ρ)π(ρ)p^*(\rho)\ \propto\ \exp\left(-\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]\right)L\left(Y\mid R,\mathcal{Z},\rho\right)\pi(\rho)p∗(ρ) ∝ exp(−ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)])L(Y∣R,Z,ρ)π(ρ)

Taking minus the logarithm and dropping the additive constant (the log of the normalizing integral in equation (13) and of the marginal likelihood, neither of which depends on ρ\rhoρ):

U(ρ)=−log⁡p∗(ρ)+const=1ξf[d,Φ(ρ)]−log⁡L(Y∣R,Z,ρ)−log⁡π(ρ)\mathcal{U}(\rho)=-\log p^*(\rho)+\text{const}=\frac{1}{\xi}f\left[d,\Phi(\rho)\right]-\log L\left(Y\mid R,\mathcal{Z},\rho\right)-\log\pi(\rho)U(ρ)=−logp∗(ρ)+const=ξ1​f[d,Φ(ρ)]−logL(Y∣R,Z,ρ)−logπ(ρ)

which is the target equation. Formally, −f/ξ-f/\xi−f/ξ enters exactly like an additional log-likelihood term, so standard software for Bayesian posteriors (Stan with the NUTS sampler) can be used: it needs only U\mathcal{U}U and its gradient, never the normalizing constant. Parameter values at which the plan ddd does well have high potential energy and are visited less often. The gradient of the first term is available because, for fixed ddd, the paths of ZZZ, UUU and VVV are fixed and fff is linear in θi\theta^iθi and γi\gamma^iγi, which are smooth functions of ρ\rhoρ by equation (11). Two notational points: π(ρ)\pi(\rho)π(ρ) here is the prior density of the regression parameters, not the baseline distribution π\piπ of φ\varphiφ in equation (10), and LLL stands for the product of the likelihoods of the two regressions. As ξ→∞\xi\to\inftyξ→∞ the first term vanishes and the sampler returns the ordinary posterior.

This is the calibration condition that pins down Brazil's own shadow price of emissions, PeeP^{ee}Pee, by revealed preference. The left side is a model object: start the model at the observed state (Xt‾o,Zt‾o)(X^o_{\underline{t}},Z^o_{\underline{t}})(Xt​o​,Zt​o​) in t‾=1995\underline{t}=1995t​=1995, feed in the cattle price path realized between 1995 and 2008, set transfers to zero so that Pe=PeeP^e=P^{ee}Pe=Pee by equation (9), solve the planner problem and add up the predicted change in agricultural area over all sites up to tˉ=2008\bar{t}=2008tˉ=2008. The right side is the observed increase in agricultural area in the biome over the same window. It is one equation in one unknown.

The solution is well defined because predicted deforestation falls monotonically as the emissions price rises: a higher PeP^ePe raises the cost of clearing (γi\gamma^iγi tons per hectare) and of keeping pasture (κ\kappaκ tons per hectare per year) in equation (8). At Pe=0P^e=0Pe=0 the model clears far more than observed, at a very high price it clears nothing, so some intermediate value matches the data; it is found by a one-dimensional search. Conceptually this is a one-moment method-of-moments estimate. Only the aggregate is matched; the allocation of clearing across sites is not targeted and serves as a check of fit.

The identifying assumption is that 1995–2008 land use is the outcome of the planner's optimization with a time-invariant price, with all other parameters correct; any omitted benefit or cost of clearing is absorbed into PeeP^{ee}Pee. This also explains why PeeP^{ee}Pee changes with the specification: under ambiguity aversion the planner clears more cautiously for a given price, so a lower PeeP^{ee}Pee (4.8 instead of 6.8 at ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1) is needed to reproduce the same history. Counterfactuals then set Pe=Pee+bP^e=P^{ee}+bPe=Pee+b.

A perpetual interest stream at rate δ\deltaδ on a deposit is worth the deposit itself when discounting is also at δ\deltaδ, whatever the value of τf\tau_fτf​. The equivalence relies on the fund's interest rate being equal to Brazil's discount rate.
